result.summary: Juno, angry that Semele is pregnant by Jupiter, disguises herself as Semele's old nurse Beroë and persuades her to ask Jupiter to appear in his full divine majesty. Jupiter, bound by an oath on the Styx, grants the request with grief and prepares his thunderbolts.

scenes.title: Juno resolves to destroy Semele
scenes.summary: Juno, angered by Semele's affair and pregnancy, rails against her and vows to have Jupiter himself bring her to ruin. Others meanwhile debate her severity.
scenes.stakes: Juno's honor as queen and wife is wounded; Semele is in danger of Juno's revenge.

scenes.title: Juno as Beroë tricks Semele
scenes.summary: Juno descends in a cloud, disguises herself as the old nurse Beroë, and plants doubts in Semele, urging her to demand Jupiter come in his full majesty.
scenes.stakes: Semele risks being deceived into destroying herself.

scenes.title: Jupiter's fatal oath
scenes.summary: Semele asks a favor, and Jupiter swears by the Styx to grant it. She asks to see him as Juno does; he groans, bound by his oath, and goes up to gather his storm and thunderbolt.
scenes.stakes: Semele's life, and Jupiter's oath on the Styx that he cannot break.

alias_notes.explanation: Juno disguises herself as Semele's old nurse Beroë.

notable_quotes.reason: The hasty words that cannot be recalled capture the tragedy of the rash wish.
Juno's insidious line plants the suspicion that destroys Semele.

analysis.text: Divine jealousy works through deceit, turning a mortal's own desire and a god's binding oath into instruments of ruin.
The sacred oath by the Styx reflects ancient views of oaths as unbreakable, even for gods.

legacy.text: Semele's death and the birth of Bacchus from this story fed later art and opera, including Handel's Semele (1744).

fun_facts.text: Ovid's Beroë is called Epidaurian, linking her to Epidaurus, the Greek city famed for its healing sanctuary.

language_notes.text: Beroë is the aged nurse of Semele whose shape Juno borrows; the disguise is how Juno gains Semele's trust.
"The Goddess" here is Juno; "strict virginity" is a loose phrase for strict chastity, the virtue some say Juno rightly defends in marriage.
Agenor was king of Tyre and father of Cadmus and Europa; Juno hates his whole line because Jupiter loved Europa, and now Semele, Cadmus's daughter.
"Tyrian mistress" means Europa, the Tyrian princess Jupiter carried off; Juno now transfers her hatred to her kin.
Juno's "if" clauses are a rhetorical oath: she stakes her title and rank on destroying Semele.
"Stygian waves" refer to the river Styx in the underworld; Saturn is Juno's father, so she swears by her parentage.
Epidaurus was a city in Greece, famous for its sanctuary of Aesculapius. Beroë is a nurse from there, so Semele would trust her.
"Ensigns" are the emblems of rank and power. Here they mean Jupiter's royal attributes, especially the thunderbolt.
The Stygian stream is the river Styx of the underworld. An oath sworn by it was binding even on the gods.
"Complaisance" means eager willingness to please. Jupiter's wish to oblige her will destroy her.
"Ties of Venus" is a euphemism for sexual love, here the marriage bed of Jupiter and Juno.

context_notes.text: Juno's trick is that Semele asks Jupiter to promise anything, then demands to see him as he appears to Juno, which mortals cannot survive.
Juno is both sister and wife of Jupiter; both were children of Saturn, and she is queen of the gods and guardian of marriage.
Juno was proud of her status as Jupiter's wife; his children by mortals, like Semele's unborn Bacchus, are living proof of his infidelity.
Juno, Jupiter's wife, is jealous of his lovers. Semele, daughter of Cadmus, is pregnant by him, and Juno intends to destroy her.
The thunderbolt is Jupiter's chief weapon. Its fire will be fatal to a mortal like Semele.

literary_notes.text: Juno's question admits that her past scolding achieved nothing, and shows her moving from words to action.
Juno bitterly says she is his sister, mocking the idea that this bond should matter to Jupiter's faithfulness.
Juno vows Semele will be destroyed by her own beloved Jupiter, which foreshadows how his promise brings her death.
The chain of "and" clauses lists each stage of Juno's disguise step by step, so the transformation seems deliberate and thorough.
The narrator calls Semele overjoyed at her own misfortune. She is happy about a request the reader knows will kill her.
The words "escaped into air" treat speech as a living thing that cannot be recalled once released.
The balanced "neither... nor" clauses show both the wish and the oath as irrevocable, so Jupiter is trapped.
